title: Political Parties
summary: This chapter explores the concept of power sharing in democracies, examining different forms and arrangements through case studies like Belgium and Sri Lanka. It analyzes majoritarianism and its consequences, compares prudential and moral reasons for power sharing, and discusses different forms of power sharing among organs of government, between governments and different social groups, and among governments at different levels. The chapter examines federalism as a form of power sharing, comparing coming-together federations like the USA with holding-together federations like India. It also covers decentralization after 1992, the three lists in the Indian Constitution, gender representation, communalism, secularism, and challenges to political parties.
hotTopics: Belgium vs Sri Lanka case studies

sections.heading: Power Sharing: Belgium and Sri Lanka
sections.para: Power sharing is a very essential part of democracy. Power sharing helps in reducing the possibility of conflict between social groups and thus ensures stability of the political order. The case study of Belgium shows how different ethnic groups have power sharing arrangements. The Belgian government recognizes the existence of regional governments and a community government. The case study of Sri Lanka shows how the Sinhalese community tried to dominate other communities. In 1956, an Act was passed to recognize Sinhala as the only official language. This created resentment among other linguistic groups. The Belgian model shows that power sharing can unite a country while the Sri Lankan model shows that the denial of power sharing can divide a country.
points: Belgium has a population of over 10 million with 59% Dutch-speaking, 40% French-speaking and 1% German-speaking people.
In Belgium, the French-speaking minority was given a special status in Brussels and the Dutch-speaking majority accepted this.
Belgium has a community government with power related to language and culture, and a regional government with power related to economic matters.
In Sri Lanka, the Sinhala community forms 74% of the population while Tamils form 18% including 13% Sri Lankan Tamils and 5% Indian Tamils.
The Sri Lankan government passed the 'Official Language Act' in 1956 making Sinhala the only official language.
The government followed a preferential policy of Sinhalese applicants for university positions and government jobs.
The Tamil parties demanded a federal arrangement with autonomy to provinces, and some even demanded a separate Tamil Eelam.
The civil war between the Sinhalese and Tamil communities lasted from 1983 to 2009 causing thousands of deaths and displacement.

An act passed in Sri Lanka in 1956 making Sinhala the only official language
A form of government in Belgium with power related to language and culture
A form of government in Belgium with power related to economic matters
A system where power is divided between central and regional governments
Self-governance or freedom from external control

sections.trick: Remember Belgium with 'B' for Both communities sharing power, while Sri Lanka with 'S' for Sinhalese dominance causing division.
sections.examPointer: CBSE often asks 3-4 marker questions comparing Belgium and Sri Lanka case studies. Focus on the power sharing arrangements in Belgium and the majoritarian policies in Sri Lanka.

sections.heading: Majoritarianism and Its Consequences
sections.para: Majoritarianism is a belief that the majority community should be able to rule a country in whichever way it wants, by disregarding the wishes and needs of the minority. This is a very dangerous and problematic concept in a democracy. In a democracy, the majority should always work with the minority to resolve differences in a manner that accommodates the interests of all. The consequences of majoritarianism in Sri Lanka led to alienation and resentment among the Tamil community. The Sri Lankan government adopted majoritarian policies to establish Sinhala supremacy. The Tamils felt that their interests and identity were being ignored. This led to the demand for a separate state and eventually a civil war that lasted for nearly 25 years. This shows that majoritarianism can be very destructive and can lead to the disintegration of a country.
points: Majoritarianism believes that the majority community should be able to rule the country in whichever way it wants.
In a democracy, the majority should always work with the minority to resolve differences.
The Sri Lankan government adopted majoritarian policies to establish Sinhala supremacy.
The Tamils felt that their interests and identity were being ignored.
The Tamils launched parties and struggles for the recognition of Tamil as an official language and for regional autonomy.
The civil war between the Sinhalese and Tamil communities lasted from 1983 to 2009.
The conflict led to thousands of deaths and displacement of people.
The conflict also led to the economic backwardness of the country.

sections.heading: Prudential and Moral Reasons for Power Sharing
sections.para: Power sharing is valuable for both prudential and moral reasons. Prudential reasons are based on the belief that power sharing will bring better outcomes. Power sharing reduces the possibility of conflict between social groups and ensures stability of the political order. It also improves the quality of decision making by including diverse perspectives. Moral reasons are based on the principle that all groups have a right to be consulted on decisions that affect them. Power sharing is the very spirit of democracy. A democratic rule involves sharing power with those affected by its exercise, and who have to live with its effects. People have a right to be consulted on how they are to be governed. The principle of power sharing also involves respect for diversity and the accommodation of social diversities.

sections.heading: Forms of Power Sharing
sections.para: Power sharing takes many forms in modern democracies. It can be among different organs of government, between governments and different social groups, and among governments at different levels. Among different organs of government, power is shared among the legislature, executive and judiciary. This is called horizontal distribution of power. It allows different organs of government to put a check on each other. Between governments and different social groups, power can be shared among different social groups such as linguistic groups, religious groups or ethnic groups. This ensures that no single group can dominate others. Among governments at different levels, power can be shared between the central government and state governments. This is called vertical distribution of power. It allows different levels of government to have their own jurisdictions and areas of functioning.

This ensures that no single group can dominate others.
Among governments at different levels, power can be shared between the central government and state governments.
This is called vertical distribution of power.

sections.heading: Federalism: Coming-together vs Holding-together Federations
sections.para: Federalism is a form of government in which power is divided between a central authority and constituent units of the country. There are two types of federations: coming-together federations and holding-together federations. In coming-together federations, independent units come together on their own to form a bigger unit. They retain their individual identities and have equal powers. The USA, Switzerland and Australia are examples of coming-together federations. In holding-together federations, a large country decides to divide its power between the central government and state governments. The central government is more powerful than the state governments. India, Spain and Belgium are examples of holding-together federations. The central government holds most of the power in these federations and the state governments have limited powers. The state governments in holding-together federations are created to accommodate regional differences and to prevent disintegration of the country.

sections.heading: Federalism in India: Features and Evolution
sections.para: India is a holding-together federation with a strong central government. The Constitution of India provides for a federal system of government with a unitary bias. The Indian federal system has several features. The Constitution divides power between the central government and state governments through three lists: the Union List, State List and Concurrent List. The Union List contains subjects on which only the central government can make laws. The State List contains subjects on which only state governments can make laws. The Concurrent List contains subjects on which both central and state governments can make laws. The central government has more powers than the state governments. The central government can change the boundaries of states, can create new states and can even dismiss state governments in certain situations. The federal system in India has evolved over time. The process of decentralization after 1992 has strengthened federalism by giving more powers to local governments.

The Constitution of India provides for a federal system of government with a unitary bias.

sections.heading: Decentralization after 1992
sections.para: Decentralization is the process of transferring power from central to local governments. In India, the process of decentralization was strengthened after 1992. The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments were passed in 1992 to give more powers to local governments. The 73rd Amendment established Panchayati Raj institutions in rural areas, while the 74th Amendment established municipalities in urban areas. These amendments made it mandatory for all states to have Panchayati Raj institutions and municipalities. The amendments reserved seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women in these institutions. The local governments now have their own budgets and can make decisions on local matters like water supply, sanitation, roads, and local markets. The decentralization process has strengthened federalism in India by making local governments more powerful and accountable to the people.

sections.heading: Gender and Politics: Sexual Division of Labour
sections.para: Gender is a social construct that defines roles and expectations for men and women in society. The sexual division of labour refers to the division of work between men and women, assigning different tasks to each. In most families, women do most of the work inside the home while men do most of the work outside the home. This division of labour is not natural but is created by society. Women's work is often not recognized as work and is not paid for. This is called the 'double burden' of women, who have to do both paid work and unpaid household work. Political representation of women is also very low in most countries. In India, women constitute about 50% of the population but their representation in Parliament is only about 15%. The women's movement has been demanding greater representation of women in politics and public life. The Women's Reservation Bill, which seeks to reserve 33% of seats in Parliament and state legislatures for women, has been pending for many years.

sections.heading: Communalism and Secularism
sections.para: Communalism is a belief that religion is the only basis for social community. It involves the belief that people who follow the same religion have common interests, which are different from those of followers of other religions. Communalism can lead to conflict between different religious groups. It can also lead to the dominance of one religious group over others. Secularism, on the other hand, is a principle that separates religion from the state. It ensures that the state does not favor any religion and treats all religions equally. In India, secularism is one of the basic features of the Constitution. The Indian state does not have an official religion and guarantees freedom of religion to all citizens. However, communalism remains a challenge in India, with occasional outbreaks of violence between different religious groups. The state must take measures to promote communal harmony and prevent communal violence.

sections.heading: Caste in Politics
sections.para: Caste is a social system that divides people into hierarchical groups based on birth. In India, caste has been a major factor in politics. Political parties often use caste identities to mobilize voters. They promise to represent the interests of particular castes and offer them various benefits in return for their support. This has led to the politicization of caste. On the positive side, caste has been used to fight against caste discrimination and oppression. The Dalit movement has used caste identity to demand equal rights and dignity for Dalits. The reservation policy in India, which reserves seats in educational institutions and government jobs for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, is based on caste. However, the use of caste in politics has also led to casteism, which is the belief that caste is the only basis of social community. Casteism can lead to conflict between different castes and can prevent the development of a unified national identity.

sections.heading: Challenges to Political Parties
sections.para: Political parties play a crucial role in a democracy, but they face several challenges. One major challenge is the lack of internal democracy. Many parties do not hold regular internal elections and decisions are often taken by a small group of leaders. This leads to concentration of power in the hands of a few. Another challenge is dynastic succession, where power is passed within a family from one generation to the next. Many political parties are dominated by families, and leadership positions are often reserved for family members. A third challenge is the role of money and muscle power in politics. Political parties often rely on wealthy donors and criminal elements for funding and support. This leads to corruption and criminalization of politics. These challenges undermine the democratic functioning of political parties and reduce their accountability to the people. Reforms are needed to make political parties more democratic and accountable.

sections.heading: Accountable, Responsive and Legitimate Government
sections.para: A democratic government must be accountable, responsive and legitimate. Accountability means that the government must answer to the people for its actions and decisions. It must be transparent and open to scrutiny. Responsiveness means that the government must respond to the needs and demands of the people. It must be sensitive to public opinion and be willing to change its policies if necessary. Legitimacy means that the government must have the consent of the governed. It must be seen as rightful and just by the people. A legitimate government is one that is elected through free and fair elections and respects the rights and freedoms of its citizens. Economic growth and inequality are important factors in determining the legitimacy of a government. While economic growth is important, it must be accompanied by reduction in inequality to ensure that the benefits of growth are shared by all. Dignity and freedom are also essential for a legitimate government. The government must respect the dignity of all citizens and protect their freedom and rights.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the majoritarianism in Sri Lanka and its consequences.
boardQuestions.answer: In Sri Lanka, the Sinhala community formed the majority and the government adopted majoritarian policies to favour them. In 1956, an Act was passed to recognise Sinhala as the only official language. This discriminated against the Tamil minority who were mostly from northern Sri Lanka. The Tamils felt that their language and culture were neglected. This led to tension between the Sinhalese and Tamil communities. The situation worsened with the rise of militant groups among the Tamils. The government responded with military action, leading to a civil war that lasted for about 25 years. This shows how majoritarianism can lead to division and conflict in a country.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the different forms of power sharing in modern democracies.
boardQuestions.answer: Power sharing in modern democracies takes several forms to ensure that power is distributed and not concentrated in one hand. The first form is horizontal distribution of power where power is shared among different organs of government like the legislature, executive, and judiciary. Each organ checks the other to maintain balance. The second form is vertical distribution where power is shared among different levels of government - central, state, and local. This is seen in federal systems like India. The third form is community power sharing where different social groups share power through representation in government. Belgium is an example where community governments represent the interests of different linguistic groups. The fourth form is political parties where different groups compete for power and represent diverse interests. Power sharing can also be among various pressure groups and movements. These forms ensure that no single group dominates and all voices are heard in the democratic process.

boardQuestions.question: What is the difference between coming-together federations and holding-together federations? Give one example of each.
boardQuestions.answer: Coming-together federations are formed when independent states come together on their own to form a bigger unit. In such federations, the central government tends to have more power and the constituent states have less autonomy. The states have the right to secede from the federation. An example is the United States of America where 13 independent states came together to form a federal government. Holding-together federations are formed when a large country decides to divide its power between the central government and state governments. In such federations, the central government is usually more powerful and the states have limited autonomy. The states do not have the right to secede. An example is India where the central government holds more power and the states are subordinate to it. Most federations in the world are holding-together federations.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the decentralisation of power after 1992 in India.
boardQuestions.answer: Decentralisation of power in India took a significant step forward after the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments in 1992. The 73rd Amendment established Panchayati Raj institutions in rural areas while the 74th Amendment established Municipalities in urban areas. These amendments gave constitutional status to local self-governance. The 73rd Amendment provided for a three-tier system of Panchayats at village, intermediate, and district levels. It reserved seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women. The 74th Amendment established Municipalities including Nagar Panchayats, Municipal Councils, and Municipal Corporations. It also reserved seats for women and weaker sections. These institutions were given powers and responsibilities for local development including planning, implementation, and monitoring of schemes. The state governments were required to devolve funds, functions, and functionaries to these institutions. This decentralisation aimed to empower local communities and ensure participatory democracy.

boardQuestions.question: Discuss the Union List, State List, and Concurrent List with examples of subjects in each.
boardQuestions.answer: The Union List contains subjects on which only the central government can make laws. These subjects are of national importance. Examples include defence, foreign affairs, banking, currency, and communications. The State List contains subjects on which only state governments can make laws. These subjects are of local importance. Examples include police, public health, agriculture, and irrigation. The Concurrent List contains subjects on which both central and state governments can make laws. Examples include education, marriage, divorce, bankruptcy, and forests. If there is a conflict between central and state laws on a concurrent subject, the central law prevails. This division of powers ensures that both levels of government can function effectively within their respective jurisdictions.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the concept of sexual division of labour and its implications.
boardQuestions.answer: Sexual division of labour refers to the division of work based on gender where women do more unpaid work than men. This includes household chores, childcare, and care of the elderly. Men usually do paid work outside the home. This division is not natural but socially constructed. It has several implications. First, it reduces women's participation in the workforce and limits their economic opportunities. Second, it increases women's workload as they have to manage both paid and unpaid work. Third, it reinforces gender stereotypes where women are seen as caregivers and men as breadwinners. Fourth, it contributes to gender inequality as women's work is often undervalued and not recognized economically. Feminist movements have challenged this division and demanded equal sharing of responsibilities between men and women.

boardQuestions.question: What is communalism? How does it pose a challenge to democracy?
boardQuestions.answer: Communalism is the belief that religion is the basis of social community and that people of one religion have common interests. It involves the assertion that one's religion is superior to others and that religious identity should determine political, social, and economic life. Communalism poses several challenges to democracy. First, it undermines the principle of secularism which is essential for democracy. Second, it leads to social division and conflict as communities are pitted against each other. Third, it can lead to violence and riots as seen in India's history. Fourth, it distorts the political process as politicians often use religious sentiments to mobilize voters. Fifth, it marginalizes minority groups and denies them equal rights. To counter communalism, democratic societies need to promote inter-faith harmony, strengthen secular institutions, and ensure equal rights for all citizens regardless of their religion.

boardQuestions.question: Discuss the challenges faced by political parties in India.
boardQuestions.answer: Political parties in India face several challenges that affect their functioning and democratic representation. The first challenge is lack of internal democracy where decisions are taken by a few leaders and ordinary members have little say. This leads to concentration of power in the hands of a few. The second challenge is dynastic succession where power is passed within families from one generation to the next. This limits opportunities for new leaders and reduces accountability. The third challenge is money and muscle power where parties depend on wealthy candidates and criminals who can fund campaigns and use violence to win elections. This corrupts the electoral process. The fourth challenge is limited choice for voters as most parties have similar agendas and fail to address diverse needs. The fifth challenge is the lack of transparency in party funding and functioning. To address these challenges, political parties need to strengthen internal democracy, promote merit-based leadership, reduce dependence on money and muscle power, and be more responsive to people's needs.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the conditions required for a party to be recognised as a national party or state party.
boardQuestions.answer: For a party to be recognised as a national party, it must meet any one of the following conditions: (i) It wins 2% of seats in the Lok Sabha from at least 3 different states, (ii) It secures at least 6% of votes in four or more states in the last Lok Sabha elections and wins at least 4 seats in the Lok Sabha, (iii) It wins 3% of seats in the Assembly elections in at least three states, or (iv) It is recognized as a state party in at least four states. For a party to be recognised as a state party, it must meet any one of the following conditions: (i) It wins at least one seat in the Lok Sabha from the state, (ii) It wins at least 3% of seats in the Assembly elections in the state, or (iii) It secures at least 6% of votes in the state in the last Assembly elections and wins at least one seat in the Assembly. Recognition as a national or state party gives parties certain privileges like access to election symbols, time on state-owned media, and other electoral advantages.
